text: Ines chopped two onions and a carrot for a stew, following the steps on the recipe card. She put the pan on the stove at medium heat and added a spoon of oil. While it heated, she checked the cupboard for rice and counted three bags. She added the onions and stirred them every minute or so, then the carrot. Her feet were on the cold tiles, so she fetched her slippers. She thought about whether to buy more rice on Thursday and decided it could wait until the following week. After twenty minutes she turned the heat down and put the lid on.

Bram washed the lettuce in the sink and laid the leaves on a towel to dry. The recipe said to toast the pine nuts first, so he put a small pan on the stove and shook it now and then. He sliced a cucumber into rounds of about the same thickness and put them in a bowl. His shoulder clicked when he reached for the olive oil on the top shelf. He measured three spoons of oil and one of vinegar into a jar, added salt, and shook it. He considered adding mustard, then left it out, and set the table for one.

Dara caught the eight-fifteen train, as she did most weekdays. She found a seat by the window facing backwards and put her bag on her lap. The carriage was about half full. She took out her phone and read the news headlines, then the weather forecast, which said cloud with a chance of showers later. Her left foot had gone slightly numb, so she shifted her weight. At the fourth stop a man with a bicycle got on and stood by the doors. She thought about which emails she needed to answer first and made a short list in her head.

Oren walked to the bus stop at seven forty and checked the timetable on the post. The next bus was due in six minutes. He stood under the shelter and zipped his jacket to the top. A woman next to him was reading a paperback. Oren looked at the traffic, then at the sign above the bakery across the road, which listed the opening hours. The bus arrived two minutes late. He tapped his card, took a seat halfway down on the left, and put his headphones in. He thought about whether he had left the window open at home and decided he had not.

Una's brother called on Wednesday evening to ask for the address of the hardware shop she had mentioned. She gave him the street name and said it was next to the post office. He asked what time it closed, and she said six, she thought, but that he could check online. They talked for a few minutes about the weather and about a cousin who was moving to another town. Una held the phone with her shoulder while she folded towels. Her neck got stiff, so she switched sides. After the call she wrote a reminder to buy batteries.

Kai's father called to ask how to change the time on his new oven. Kai asked him which buttons it had, and his father read them out one by one. They tried pressing and holding the clock button for three seconds, which did not work, and then the settings button, which did. The display blinked and his father set it to the right time. Kai was standing at the window while they talked and noticed that the neighbor's car had been moved. His father mentioned that the bin collection day had changed to Tuesday. Kai said he would put it in his calendar.

Esme arrived at the office at nine and hung her coat on the rack by the door. She turned on her computer and waited while it updated. Then she opened the spreadsheet from the day before and continued entering the figures from the invoices, one row at a time. After an hour her eyes felt dry, so she got up and filled her water bottle at the tap in the kitchen. A colleague asked her where the stapler was, and she pointed to the shelf. She thought about whether to take lunch at twelve or at one and chose one.

Gus spent the morning at the warehouse checking a delivery against the order sheet. He counted forty boxes of screws, twelve boxes of hinges, and six rolls of tape, and ticked each line with a pencil. One box of hinges was the wrong size, so he wrote a note to call the supplier. He moved the boxes onto the correct shelves with a trolley. His hands were a little dusty, so he wiped them on his trousers. At eleven he had a cup of tea and went through the next order, which was due on Friday.

Pia went out into the garden on Saturday morning to cut the grass. She checked the mower's fuel and topped it up from the red can in the shed. The grass was dry enough. She mowed the front section in straight lines, then the back, emptying the grass box twice into the compost bin. Her arms vibrated a little from the handle. After that she trimmed the edges with shears and swept the path. She thought about moving the pots of herbs to the sunnier side of the patio and did it before lunch.

Lior spent an hour in the garden tying the tomato plants to their canes with green string. He worked along the row, one plant at a time, looping the string loosely so it would not cut the stems. He pinched out a few side shoots with his fingers. The soil was damp from the night's rain, and his knees left marks in it. He noted that the beans needed more support and that the lettuce would be ready in about a week. Then he rinsed his hands at the outdoor tap and went inside to put the kettle on.

Vera went to the clinic for a routine blood test. She gave her name at the desk and was told to take a seat. There were four other people waiting. She read a leaflet about vaccinations while she waited and then looked at the clock, which said ten past ten. A nurse called her after about fifteen minutes. Vera rolled up her left sleeve and looked at the wall while the nurse took the sample. She pressed a small cotton pad on her arm for a minute. The nurse said the results would be ready in five days.

Femi had an appointment at the clinic to renew his prescription. The doctor asked him a few questions about how the medicine had been working, checked his blood pressure, and typed some notes. The cuff squeezed his arm and then loosened. The doctor printed the prescription and signed it. Femi asked if he could get three months at once, and the doctor said yes. On the way out he booked his next check-up for the spring. He thought about which pharmacy was open on Saturdays and walked to the one near the station.

The post arrived at eleven: a bank statement, a catalog from a garden center, and a leaflet about a change to the recycling collection. Noor opened the statement at the kitchen table and checked the list of payments against her own notes. They matched. She put the statement in the folder in the second drawer. The catalog she put on the pile by the sofa. The leaflet said that glass would now be collected every other week. She stuck it to the fridge with a magnet, then rinsed her mug and put it on the rack.

A parcel came for Ivo on Tuesday: the replacement filter for his coffee machine that he had ordered the week before. He opened the box with a knife and read the instructions on the leaflet. He removed the old filter, rinsed the new one under the tap for thirty seconds as the leaflet said, and fitted it into the water tank. He ran a cycle of plain water through the machine to flush it. His sleeve got wet at the cuff, so he rolled it up. He flattened the box and put it with the recycling.

Zola fed the cat at seven, as usual, half a pouch of food and a handful of dry biscuits. She refilled the water bowl and washed the old one in the sink. The cat ate and then went to sit on the windowsill. Zola checked the calendar and saw that his vaccination was due next month, so she wrote a note to call the vet. She swept a few stray biscuits from the floor with the small brush. Her back twinged slightly when she bent down. Then she made her own breakfast, toast with butter, and ate it standing at the counter.

Jun took the dog out for his usual walk around the block at six in the evening. They went left at the gate, past the post box, along the row of houses to the corner, and back by the other street. The dog stopped at the same lamp posts it always did. Jun kept the lead short near the road. He noticed that the corner shop had new opening hours posted on the door. Back home he wiped the dog's paws with a towel, hung up the lead on its hook, and filled the water bowl at the tap.

Tavi spent Saturday packing books into boxes for the move on Monday. She put the heavy books in small boxes and the paperbacks in larger ones, as the moving company had suggested, and wrote the room on the side of each box with a marker: study, living room, bedroom. Her fingers were black from the ink. She counted fourteen boxes by the afternoon. She checked the list of things to do before the move and ticked off the gas meter reading. Then she taped the last box shut and stacked it by the door.

Eli unpacked the kitchen boxes in his new flat on Sunday. He put the plates in the cupboard above the sink and the pans in the drawer under the oven. The cutlery tray fitted the second drawer. He found that one box contained only baking tins, which he put on the top shelf. The cardboard left a slight dust on his hands. He folded the empty boxes flat and stacked them in the hallway to take to the recycling point. Then he made a list of things he still needed, including a bin and a bath mat.

Wren cycled to the library on Saturday morning to return two books. She took the route along the main road and then turned onto the side street with the bike lane. At the library she locked her bicycle to the rack outside and went in. She put the books through the returns slot and looked at the new arrivals shelf. She borrowed one book about the history of maps. Outside she noticed her back tire was slightly soft, so she decided to pump it up when she got home. She cycled back the same way.

Amir spent the afternoon servicing his bicycle in the yard. He turned it upside down on the grass, cleaned the chain with a rag, and applied a few drops of oil to each link. He checked the brake pads, which still had some wear left on them, and tightened the bolt on the saddle. The oil left a smudge on his thumb. He pumped both tires to the pressure printed on the side. Then he took it for a short ride around the block to check the gears, and put it back in the shed.

Hana went to the market on Saturday with a list: potatoes, onions, apples, eggs, and cheese. She went to the vegetable stall first, then the egg stall, which had medium and large; she took large. At the cheese stall she asked for a quarter of the hard cheese and paid with coins. The bag got heavy on her shoulder, so she moved it to the other side. She checked her list again and saw that she had forgotten the apples, so she went back to the fruit stall. Then she walked home the usual way.

Teo set up his stall at the market at seven. He unfolded the table, laid out the crates of potatoes, carrots and cabbages, and wrote the prices on the chalkboard. He put the scale at the front and checked it with a one-kilo weight. The first customers came at about eight. He weighed and bagged the vegetables and gave change from the tin. Around ten he moved the cabbages to the front because the carrots were running low. His feet were tired from standing, so he sat on a crate for a few minutes between customers.

It rained all afternoon, so Cleo stayed in and sorted the papers on her desk. She made three piles: bills, letters, and things to throw away. She put the bills in date order and filed them in the folder. She shredded the old bank letters. Every so often she looked out of the window at the rain on the street, then went back to the next paper. Her tea went cold, and she drank it anyway. By five o'clock the desk was clear except for the lamp and a pen, and she put the folder back on the shelf.

Sami spent the rainy afternoon fixing a dripping tap in the bathroom. He turned off the water under the sink, unscrewed the handle, and took out the old washer, which was worn flat. He compared it with the new ones in the packet and found one of the same size. He fitted it, screwed the handle back on, and turned the water on again. The tap stopped dripping. His knees were stiff from kneeling on the tiles, so he stood up and stretched. He put the tools back in the box and wiped the sink.

Nell's friend came round on Thursday evening to borrow a folding table for a party. They carried it from the cupboard under the stairs to the friend's car and fitted it into the back after folding down one of the seats. Nell's friend stayed for a cup of tea. They talked about the new timetable for the local buses and about a film each of them had seen on television. The friend mentioned she would bring the table back on Sunday. Nell wrote Sunday on the kitchen calendar. The friend left at eight.

Quin's friend came over on Saturday to help him put together a new bookshelf. They laid out the pieces on the living room floor and followed the diagram step by step. Quin held the side panels while his friend put in the screws. They got step six wrong the first time and had to undo two screws. The small hex key left a mark on Quin's palm. After an hour the bookshelf was standing. They pushed it against the wall, and Quin checked it with a spirit level. Then his friend went home and Quin put the books on it.

Rhea took her car to the garage on Monday morning for its yearly service. She handed the keys to the man at the desk, who asked for her phone number and said it would be ready by four. She walked to the cafe on the corner and worked on her laptop for a while. At half past three the garage called to say the car was done: new oil, a new air filter, and the tires checked. She paid at the desk. On the drive home she noticed that the brakes felt the same as before.

Tavi filled up his car at the petrol station on the way home. He chose pump four, filled the tank until the nozzle clicked, and checked the price on the display. Then he used the air machine to check the tire pressure, which was slightly low on the front left, and added a little air. His hands smelled faintly of petrol, so he used a paper towel from the dispenser. He paid inside with his card and bought a bottle of water. He thought about whether to wash the car at the weekend and decided to see what the weather did.

Bea arrived at the school gate at three fifteen to collect her son. She stood with the other parents by the fence. The doors opened at three twenty and the children came out in lines with their teachers. Her son had his coat over his arm and a painting rolled up in his hand. She asked him what he had had for lunch, and he said pasta. They walked home the usual way, past the park. At home she put the painting on the table and asked him to hang up his coat on the hook by the door.

Rafa picked his daughter up from school on Friday. He parked two streets away because the road outside was full and walked the rest of the way. His daughter came out with a note from the teacher about a trip to the museum next month, which needed a signature. On the walk back to the car she told him that her class was learning about volcanoes. Rafa's car keys were in the wrong pocket, so it took him a moment to find them. At home he signed the note and put it in her book bag.

Yara went to the lake on Saturday afternoon to swim some lengths. She left her towel and bag on the grass by the jetty and walked in from the shallow end. The water was cool. She swam out to the second buoy and back five times, which she estimated was about a kilometer. Her shoulders were a bit tired by the end. She dried off on the grass, put on her clothes over her swimsuit, and drank some water from the bottle. She checked the time and saw she had half an hour before the bus.

Zeb took his nephew to the beach for the afternoon. They put up the windbreak with a mallet, spread out the towels, and put the cool box in the shade. His nephew built a sandcastle near the water, and Zeb helped him dig a moat. The tide was going out. Zeb put more sun cream on the back of his neck. At four they packed up, shook the sand off the towels, and carried everything back to the car park. On the way home they stopped at a garage for petrol and bought two sandwiches.
